units.ci: Observing how materials change helps us make sense of the physical world.
units.lo:
The observable properties of solids and liquids
How heating and cooling can change the state of materials
How scientific thinking helps us solve everyday problems

builtFrom.ci: Observing how materials change helps us make sense of the physical world.
builtFrom.lo: Observable properties of solids and liquids; How heating and cooling change state; Scientific thinking helps solve everyday problems

s.d: Students use teacher-supplied photographs of wet clay, dry clay and fired ceramic to explain the changes. In one 50 minute lesson, pairs place the images in a short digital book and record an explanation beside each. Preparation takes 10 minutes if photographs from the art project are ready. Students listen back with a partner and re-record any claim that all changes can be undone by cooling. They finish with an audio comparison between clay firing and the class ice investigation.
s.why: Recorded explanations beside stage photographs make it easy to hear and revise students' thinking about different kinds of change.
s.quote: Students will investigate how water, air, and especially heat affect clay, changing it from a soft and workable material into a hard and durable ceramic object through the firing process.
s.link: This draws together the art investigation and ice investigation to distinguish melting from changes that cooling does not undo.

s.d: Students photograph an ice cube in a shallow tray every minute while watching it melt. Keep the device still on a simple stand and include a paper time label beside the tray. Allow one 50 minute lesson and 10 minutes beforehand to check the camera and gather trays. Students play the photographs as a short movie, noticing when edges soften and water spreads. They finish by choosing two moments that show how adding heat changes solid water into liquid water.
s.why: Rapid playback makes gradual melting visible, helping students support explanations with changes they can actually see.
s.quote: Assessment: investigating ice melting or water freezing in a sealed bag and explaining their observations
s.link: This adds a replayable record to the planned ice investigation so students can revisit changes that were slow to notice.

s.d: Students photograph the same solid and liquid samples in differently shaped clear containers. In pairs, they add the photographs to a shared device's Freeform board and group them by what stays the same or changes. Plan 45 minutes, with 10 minutes beforehand to gather safe samples and containers. Students zoom in on details and move photographs when a partner challenges a choice. They keep their first and revised arrangements on separate parts of the board, then explain which observation changed their thinking.
s.activity: Comparing properties of solids and liquids
s.why: Movable photographs let students regroup real evidence and revisit examples that challenge their first sorting decisions.

s.d: Students collect examples of solids and sealed containers of liquids, then predict how a camera might sort them. In a 45 minute lesson, help groups train one shared image classifier with two labelled groups of examples. Allow 15 minutes beforehand to check camera access and practise adding images. Students test unfamiliar examples and move the same container against different backgrounds. They compare the results with real observations of shape and pouring, then explain why the camera sometimes gets it wrong.
s.why: Testing a camera classifier helps students notice why appearance alone cannot reliably identify solids and liquids.
s.quote: L1 - What clues help us classify a material as a solid or a liquid?
s.link: This extends the initial classification activity by testing whether visible clues are enough to identify solids and liquids.

s.d: Students compare ice melting in two safe classroom spots, one warmer and one cooler. With help, they code a micro:bit to display its temperature when a button is pressed. Allow two lessons and 15 minutes to check the simple code and gather trays. Move the board between spots, let readings settle, and keep it dry beside rather than inside each tray. Explain that it reads board temperature, not ice temperature. Students compare these rough local readings with melting observations before recommending where to keep ice.
s.activity: Heat and materials in real life
s.why: Live temperature readings help students check whether a warmer location also makes ice melt more quickly.
s.quote: L3 - How can understanding heat and materials help us in real life?
s.link: This builds on heating and cooling investigations by using measurements to check advice about where ice will last longer.

stem.d: Students build ice-cube shelters around identical cups using cardboard, foil, fabric scraps and tape. Across two lessons, they test shelters beside an uncovered cup, using equal ice cubes and measuring collected meltwater after the same time. Students enter the results into Microsoft Excel and make a column chart to compare designs. They change one feature, repeat the test under similar conditions and use the new chart to judge the improvement. Allow 15 minutes to gather materials, measuring containers and a simple results sheet.
stem.why: A shared graph helps students compare melting across designs and check whether their improvements really helped.
stem.quote: L3 - How can understanding heat and materials help us in real life?
stem.link: This turns observations from heating and cooling investigations into a practical design problem: slowing the melting of ice.

units.ci: Creativity allows people to express their understanding of the world.
units.lo:
The ways people use technology to express their creativity.
How texts and images work together.
How technology influences our creativity.

builtFrom.ci: Creativity allows people to express their understanding of the world.
builtFrom.lo: The ways people use technology to express creativity; How texts and images work together; How technology influences our creativity

s.d: Students record short musical parts inspired by different features of a picture book image. Use the pentatonic notes already explored in Music, recording one part at a time into the same project. In two 40 minute lessons, groups listen back and adjust which parts are loud, quiet or repeated. Teacher preparation takes about 10 minutes to practise recording and playing back two tracks. Each group presents its combined recording and explains how the sounds express its understanding of the image.
s.why: Recording separate musical parts lets students hear, adjust and combine their ideas rather than relying on a single live performance.
s.quote: Music: students worked in small groups to create a composition inspired by a picture book image.
s.link: This extends the image-inspired composition by letting students listen closely to how their separate musical parts work together.

s.d: Students photograph a classroom object and place the same image on two pages. They add a different short caption to each, making the object seem welcoming on one page and mysterious on the other. Give pairs one 50 minute lesson and spend five minutes beforehand checking how to add photographs and text. Partners read both versions and explain how the words changed their reading of the image. Students revise one caption and keep both pages as evidence of how text and images shape meaning together.
s.why: Comparing the same image with different words helps students see how text changes a reader's interpretation.
s.quote: How texts and images work together. How technology influences our creativity.
s.link: This makes the text and image inquiry concrete through paired versions that students can compare and revise.

s.d: Students draw a simple face and animate a change in its expression across six to eight frames. Begin with mirrors and a discussion about how the same expression might be read differently in different situations. Allow two 40 minute lessons, with 10 minutes beforehand to practise adding frames and playing the animation. Partners watch without hearing the intended meaning, then explain which moving features gave them clues. Students revise one detail and present how their animation communicates a feeling.
s.why: Frame-by-frame playback makes small changes in drawn expressions visible and gives students a clear way to test their meaning.
s.quote: Facial expression as a form of communication Term 1 - students explore how we communicate and express ourselves using our faces.
s.link: This extends the exploration of facial communication by letting students build and replay small changes in an expression.

s.d: Students draw a familiar playground place, then save a copy before changing its colours and marks. Ask them to make the second version express a different feeling about that place. Allow one 50 minute lesson, with five minutes beforehand to check how to save their work. Partners compare both versions and point to choices that changed the meaning. Students finish by explaining whether the available tools helped their idea or pulled it in a new direction.
s.why: Students compare changes to the same drawing and notice how digital tools influence their artistic choices.
s.quote: They will learn foundational skills such as taking well-composed photographs with an iPad and using the basic drawing and editing tools in apps like Brushes Redux and PicEdu.
s.link: This builds on exploring drawing tools by asking students to notice how those tools influence what they express.

s.d: Students film three short shots of a hand approaching a closed cardboard box. In pairs, they make two versions using the same footage, changing shot length and adding or removing recorded tapping sounds. Allow two 45 minute lessons, with 10 minutes beforehand to practise trimming clips and recording sound. Show both versions in class and ask students which feels more tense and why. Each pair explains how editing influenced its creative choices, rather than treating tension as something created only by acting.
s.why: Editing identical footage in different ways reveals how timing and sound can change the tension an audience feels.
s.quote: They also learn to analyse dramatic tension through in film and television and how/why certain elements are used.
s.link: This builds on analysing dramatic tension by letting students test how editing and sound influence an audience.

stem.d: Students build a miniature stage from cardboard boxes, tracing paper and removable cardboard flaps, then use a torch to create a tense scene with a paper figure. Across two lessons, they use a Micro:bit programmed to display its light reading, keeping it in the same stage position while testing different flap openings. They record readings alongside observations of the shadows, then improve one opening to achieve their chosen lighting effect. Allow 15 minutes of preparation to gather materials and practise the short program that repeatedly displays the light level. Students present their improved stage and explain how the measurements helped them control the lighting, without claiming that a sensor can measure tension.
stem.why: Light readings help students compare stage designs fairly and connect physical design changes with the atmosphere they create.
stem.quote: They also learn to analyse dramatic tension through in film and television and how/why certain elements are used.
stem.link: This extends the exploration of dramatic tension through building, measuring and improving lighting for a miniature scene.

units.lo:
How needs and wants lead to new inventions
How digital devices and networks operate
Being a responsible digital citizen

builtFrom.lo:
How needs and wants lead to new inventions
How digital devices and networks operate
Being a responsible digital citizen

s.d: Students help train a teacher-controlled image classifier to distinguish a pencil from a glue stick. Spend 15 minutes beforehand checking camera access and trying two image classes, then allow one lesson. Capture only objects against a plain background, keeping students out of view. Students test the objects at different angles, tally mistakes and suggest extra examples to improve the results. They explain how the camera supplies images while software makes a prediction, and discuss whose need an object sorter might meet.
s.why: Live testing shows students how camera input and software work together, including when the software gets things wrong.

s.d: Students sort pictures of familiar digital devices by the needs or wants they meet. Allow one lesson, with 10 minutes beforehand to gather pictures of classroom devices. In pairs, students build a Popplet map with branches such as communicating, creating and playing. They connect a device to more than one branch and explain their choices to another pair. After discussing why people invent things, students move or add connections and explain one change in their thinking.
s.why: Students can rearrange their thinking and compare how one invention meets several different needs.
s.quote: Why do people invent things, and how do we design a solution for a real problem?
s.link: This extends the prior knowledge sheet by making students' connections between inventions, needs and wants easy to revisit.

s.d: Students move paper message pieces between a sender, a network device and a receiver, photographing each small move. Use one lesson and 10 minutes of prep to gather paper, markers and a simple teacher reference diagram. Explain that messages travel as data through connected devices, rather than as whole pictures floating through the air. Pairs make a short animation showing this simplified journey. They replay it with another pair, correct a missing connection and record a spoken explanation.
s.activity: How digital devices and networks operate
s.why: Animation makes an invisible message journey visible, so students can replay it and spot missing steps.
s.quote: What happens inside our computers and networks when we send a message or a picture to someone else?
s.link: This gives students a visible way to explain the planner's question about messages travelling through computers and networks.

s.d: Students program a robot to deliver a paper message between two buildings on a floor map. Allow two lessons and 15 minutes to gather tape, check connections and practise a short movement program. Pairs mark a start, destination and blocked path, then code timed rolls and turns. They test at low speed, measure where the robot stops and change one instruction at a time. Students demonstrate their improved route and explain which delivery need their invention addresses.
s.why: A moving robot gives immediate evidence of whether students' instructions solve their delivery problem.
s.quote: algorithms used to solve problems, run software, or program actions.
s.link: This connects the planner's algorithms work with its school-map robot example through a practical delivery problem.

s.d: Students create a short audio advice book about two safe or risky online situations already discussed in Library. Allow one lesson and five minutes to select fictional examples without names or personal details. Pairs draw each situation, then record what they would do and why. Partners listen without extra explanation and say whether the advice is clear enough to follow. Students rerecord one explanation and finish by explaining how a useful digital invention can also create responsibilities.
s.why: Recorded explanations let students hear their reasoning and improve safety advice after a partner responds.
s.quote: Library: In Library, students explored the theme of digital wellbeing and citizenship through stories about balancing screen time, safe internet use, and responsible online behavior.
s.link: This builds on Library discussions by asking students to explain and improve practical advice about responsible online behaviour.

stem.d: Students build a miniature reading shelter from cardboard, fabric scraps and popsticks that reduces glare without making the space too dark. Allow two lessons and 15 minutes beforehand to gather materials and prepare a Micro:bit program that displays its light reading when a button is pressed. Students place the Micro:bit in the same spot beneath each roof and compare readings under the same classroom lamp, keeping its LED face uncovered. They change one roof opening or fabric layer, retest and explain which design best meets their chosen need for light and shade.
stem.why: A light sensor helps students compare shade designs using readings rather than relying only on how bright something looks.
stem.quote: Why do people invent things, and how do we design a solution for a real problem?
stem.link: This gives students a small physical design problem where a digital sensor helps them test and improve their solution.

units.ci: The diversity of soils, rocks, and minerals shapes the way people value and use Earth's resources.
units.lo:
Soils, rocks, and minerals have observable properties that make them useful in different ways.
Earth's resources are vital for living things, including humans, and must be used responsibly.
First Nations Australians have long-standing knowledge and cultural uses of soils, rocks, and minerals.

builtFrom.ci: The diversity of soils, rocks, and minerals shapes the way people value and use Earth's resources.
builtFrom.lo: Observable properties of soils, rocks and minerals; Earth's resources are vital and must be used responsibly; First Nations knowledge of soils and rocks

s.d: Students examine equal spoonfuls of collected soil and count visible pebbles and pieces of plant matter. Keep samples separate and leave any living creatures undisturbed. Allow one lesson, with ten minutes beforehand to prepare a simple shared table in Excel. Pairs contribute their counts while the teacher helps turn the class results into column charts. Compare samples collected from the same place as well as different places. Students explain one pattern and why a small sample might not represent the whole garden bed.
s.why: A shared chart makes differences between samples easier to spot and gives students evidence for checking their first impressions.
s.quote: Local Soil Study: collect soil samples from different locations around the school or local area.
s.link: This builds on the local soil observations by bringing the class counts together for a more careful comparison.

s.d: Students build a tabletop scene showing soil, plants and flowing water using paper pieces and reusable modelling clay. Across two lessons, they photograph tiny changes to show rain carrying uncovered soil away. Spend ten minutes beforehand practising capture and playback, then keep devices still on simple stands. Partners replay their sequence and check whether the movement clearly explains what happens. They revise any confusing frames and add a second ending with ground cover protecting the soil. Finish by explaining which parts show evidence from their learning and which simplify real events.
s.why: Animating small changes helps students explain how losing soil affects living things rather than simply listing why soil matters.
s.quote: How do soils, rocks, and minerals connect living things and societies across places?
s.link: This develops the planned concluding explanation through a moving model of soil's importance and responsible care.

s.d: Students listen to a First Nations speaker in a community-endorsed source explaining a particular use of ochre or grindstones. Spend up to 15 minutes selecting a short source that is appropriate for classroom use and checking sharing permissions. Across two lessons, pairs create two pages in Book Creator using their own material observations and a link to the source. They record what they learnt, naming the community identified by the source rather than generalising across Australia. Students replay and revise their explanations without copying cultural designs or demonstrating restricted practices. Finish with a reflection on the resource's practical and cultural value.
s.why: Recorded explanations alongside credited sources let students revisit their wording and clearly separate learned knowledge from their own reflections.
s.quote: Cultural Knowledge: Students explain how First Nations Australians use a particular rock, mineral, or soil resource and reflect on its value.
s.link: This supports the planned cultural explanation while keeping First Nations voices, attribution and permissions central.

s.d: Students explore teacher-selected Street View locations near Glen Waverley and in Indonesia, looking for gardens, farms, exposed ground and building materials. Spend ten minutes beforehand checking two accessible locations with clear views. In one lesson, pairs take turns navigating and zooming without logging in or saving maps. They sketch evidence in a paper Venn diagram and distinguish observations from guesses. Prompt students to consider where plants need soil and where buildings cover it. Each pair finishes with one question about responsible resource use that the images cannot answer.
s.why: Street View lets students inspect distant landscapes closely and compare visible ways people use land without leaving the classroom.
s.quote: Comparison: Students create a Venn diagram or report comparing natural features of Australia with a neighbouring country.
s.link: This gives students close-up visual evidence for the planned comparison while keeping claims about soils and resources cautious.

s.d: Students sort three dry soil samples by visible properties, then test whether a webcam can tell them apart. Allow one lesson and 15 minutes beforehand to practise creating an image project with three labelled groups. Students help capture several views of each sample on identical trays against the same background. Test fresh views, change the lighting and discuss mistakes. Explain that the tool matches appearances, not soil ingredients or scientific identities. Students finish by recording which properties helped their own sorting more than the computer's.
s.why: Testing a webcam classifier helps students notice which visible properties are useful clues and which can mislead them.
s.quote: Science Investigation: Students classify and compare soil/rock samples, describing their observable properties.
s.link: This extends the planned sample classification by letting students test how reliably visible differences distinguish their samples.

stem.d: Students build soil-saving barriers from mesh offcuts, small stones and popsticks in shallow trays of soil, linking their designs to the investigation of soil's importance. Allow two lessons and 15 minutes to gather materials, prepare trays and practise filming with IMovie. Teams pour the same amount of water from the same height onto equally sloped trays, filming each test with a device kept safely away from splashes. They replay the clips to spot where soil escapes, change one part of the barrier and repeat under the same conditions. Students present before-and-after footage and explain whether their change kept more soil in place without simply blocking all water.
stem.why: Video replay helps students compare how their barriers behave and notice exactly where soil escapes before improving their designs.
stem.quote: Why are soils, rocks, and minerals important for living things and humans?
stem.link: This turns the planner's investigation of soil's importance into a practical design task that protects soil needed by living things.

units.th: Where We Are in Place and Time
units.ci: Land and place are represented and valued in different ways.
units.lo:
How Australia and its neighbouring regions define places
First Nations Australians have deep and ongoing connections to Country, which are spiritual, cultural, and environmental.
Places can be understood and valued in different ways, depending on cultural and historical perspectives.

builtFrom.ci: Land and place are represented and valued in different ways.
builtFrom.lo: How Australia and neighbouring regions define places; Australia's states/territories have unique identities; First Nations connections to Country

s.d: Students explore Australia and a neighbouring country, then open Street View where coverage is available. Pairs compare what they notice about roads, buildings and land with what the world map shows. Allow one lesson, with 10 minutes beforehand to check two suitable locations. Students only view and navigate, with no login or saved pins needed. They finish with a spoken explanation of what each view reveals and leaves out, remembering that one street cannot represent a whole country.
s.why: Students move between regional maps and street-level views to check how a map represents a real place.
s.quote: How can we use maps to learn about Aust and our neighbouring countries?
s.link: This builds on learning about Australia's neighbours by connecting map locations with visible features of particular places.

s.d: Students photograph their original world map before adding new learning in a different colour on paper. They upload an after photo and record an explanation of two important changes. Prompt them to explain whose views their map includes and what it still cannot show about a valued place. Allow one lesson and five minutes to prepare the class instructions. Partners listen, ask one clarifying question, and students rerecord if needed. The finished entry preserves both the visible changes and their reasons.
s.activity: Add to the original world map
s.why: Voice recordings capture students' reasons for map changes, revealing understanding that labels and colours alone might miss.
s.quote: Students are given their original world map and asked to add to it - using a different colour to show new learning.
s.link: This keeps the planned map assessment and adds students' explanations of how their understanding of place has changed.

s.d: Students listen to a teacher-selected, community-endorsed First Nations account of connection to Country. Pairs create one book page with a drawing and record their own explanation of something they learnt. They name the source and distinguish its teaching from their own thoughts. Allow one lesson and 15 minutes to select the source and check sharing permissions. Replay recordings so students can revise explanations that treat Country as only land, without copying cultural designs or retelling restricted knowledge.
s.why: Recorded reflections let students explain and revisit how a First Nations source has changed their understanding of Country.
s.quote: First Nations Australians have deep and ongoing connections to Country, which are spiritual, cultural, and environmental…
s.link: This supports exploring Country through First Nations voices, with students recording their developing understanding rather than inventing cultural knowledge.

s.d: Students move a paper arrow across a regional map, photographing small steps from Australia towards a neighbouring country. They play the images as an animation and describe the compass directions shown. Partners check the route against the map, then reshoot any misleading section. Explain that this shows relative location, not an actual travel route or journey time. Allow one lesson and 10 minutes to gather maps and arrow cut-outs. Finish by comparing how different map positions affect their direction descriptions.
s.activity: Revise the points of the compass
s.why: Animation playback makes changes in direction visible, helping students check whether their spoken route matches movement on a map.

s.d: Students build a small fictional lookout beside a beach or creek, adding paths, seating and protected vegetation. Partners walk through it as visitors and explain where access or care for the place could improve. Students change one feature, then revisit it from ground level to check the difference. Keep builds small and use an existing flat world, with 15 minutes to check access beforehand. Across two lessons, students explain how their changes balance different ways people value a place.
s.why: Students can walk through a proposed design, experience its effects and alter it after hearing a different viewpoint.
s.quote: Choose a place or feature of Australia and write and how and why people could show respect for it.
s.link: This extends the respect-for-place writing task into a small design that students can explore and improve.

stem.d: Students build a large floor map of an imaginary coastal place using cardboard landmarks, fabric water and masking-tape paths, then code a Sphero BOLT to travel between landmarks. In pairs, they test short roll commands, measuring where the robot stops and adjusting travel time or heading. They widen one tricky path or move a cardboard barrier, then test whether their change helps the robot reach its destination. Allow two lessons and 15 minutes to charge robots, gather materials and check a clear floor area. Students finish by explaining how their simplified map helps navigation but leaves out other things people might value.
stem.activity: Revise the points of the compass
stem.why: A moving robot reveals whether students' route measurements and directions work, giving them clear evidence for improving their design.

units.ci: Strategies support healthy relationships and personal growth.
units.lo:
How our words, actions and choices affect others
Ways we can solve problems and manage conflict respectfully
Why is it important to listen to feedback and use it to grow
What helps us keep going when things get tricky

builtFrom.ci: The choices and actions we make contribute to our health and wellbeing.
builtFrom.lo: What it means to be healthy; Choices and their impact on health; Actions to maintain a healthy mind and body

s.d: Students record a short explanation of how to make amends, then ask a partner for one helpful suggestion. Model feedback such as asking for a clearer next step, rather than judging the speaker. Allow five minutes to check recording access and 40 minutes for the lesson. Students listen to their first recording, practise using the suggestion and save a second attempt alongside it. They replay both and explain which feedback helped them improve and what they want to practise next.
s.why: Keeping a first attempt beside a revised recording makes it easier to hear whether feedback led to a useful change.

s.d: Students use counters or clay figures to animate someone trying a tricky task, meeting a setback and trying a different strategy. Connect this to the planner's discussion of athletes' attitudes without asking students to copy sporting footage. Spend ten minutes checking the capture and playback controls and gathering materials. Across two 40 minute lessons, pairs plan six key moments, photograph small movements and replay their animation to check whether the strategy is clear. Finish by naming the action that helped their character keep going.
s.why: Animating a setback makes students show the small actions involved in persisting, not just say that someone kept trying.

s.d: Students watch a short section of the planner's friendship video and spot a choice that affects someone else. Allow five minutes beforehand to preview the clip and choose two stopping points. In a 35 minute lesson, pause before a response and ask pairs to predict how each person might feel. Replay the moment so students can check facial expressions, words and actions against their predictions. Finish with pairs acting out a kinder response and explaining what they changed.
s.why: Pausing and replaying a shared moment helps students check what they noticed rather than rely on first impressions.
s.quote: Develop a list of things students can do to make the class friendly.
s.link: This builds on identifying friendly behaviour by examining the effects of specific choices.

s.d: Students record the same friendly sentence twice, first sounding impatient and then sounding calm. Use a made-up disagreement about sharing equipment rather than a real class conflict. Allow ten minutes to check audio recording, then run a 45 minute lesson with pairs sharing devices. Students play both recordings to another pair, who explain how the voice changes the message, then record a more respectful version. They finish with a short audio comparison explaining which response could help settle the disagreement.
s.why: Hearing the same words delivered differently makes the effect of tone easier to notice and discuss.

s.d: Students create a short Friendship Fire comic with drawings and recorded inner thoughts for both characters. Use a fictional disagreement and keep the story to three pages: the problem, a respectful response and making amends. Allow ten minutes to check drawing and audio recording, then two 40 minute lessons. Partners read the pictures first, then tap the recordings to hear feelings that were not obvious from the dialogue. Students revise one response after listening and finish by explaining how it supports a healthier friendship.
s.why: Recorded inner thoughts let readers hear two perspectives that the characters do not say aloud.
s.quote: Create a graphic novel that features a Friendship Fire.
s.link: This extends the planned graphic novel by letting readers hear both characters' unspoken perspectives.

stem.d: Students build a lightweight chariot from cardboard, straws, wheels and tape for a Sphero BOLT to pull using a loose cardboard harness that does not block rolling. Allow 15 minutes to gather materials and check a short, slow programmed route with a turn, then use two 45 minute lessons. Teams test whether their chariot carries three counters through the route without spilling, keeping the robot programme unchanged. After each run, students give one kind, specific suggestion and alter one part, such as the axle position or tray sides. They compare successful deliveries before and after the change, then explain which teamwork strategy helped when the build became tricky.
stem.why: A repeatable robot route helps students compare chariot changes while practising calm teamwork when designs fail.
stem.quote: During these tasks we were aiming to be... collaborators.
stem.link: This builds directly on the Sphero Chariot race, combining a fair design comparison with reflection on teamwork and persistence.
